blockers.description: `/gsd-autonomous --from N --to N` IS UNSAFE FOR RESUMING A MID-EXECUTION PHASE. Its plan step has NO `has_plans` gate — it calls gsd-plan-phase unconditionally and only checks has_plans afterwards. gsd-plan-phase itself only guards against replanning CLOSED phases (VERIFICATION status passed). A paused phase is not closed, so the planner would have run against Phase 206's 13 existing plans, 5 already executed, including the 206-13 disposition fence.
blockers.workaround: Use `Skill(gsd-execute-phase, "<N> --no-transition")` directly. Its workflow line 321 filters `Skip plans where has_summary: true`, so it resumes correctly — it ran exactly the 8 incomplete plans. Note the asymmetry: the discuss step DOES skip on has_context; only plan lacks the matching gate.

blockers.description: `state.begin-phase` is called by execute-phase's validate_phase step and is NOT idempotent mid-phase — it resets progress.percent to 0 and rewrites 'Plan: 1 of N'. `phase.complete` writes well-formed WRONG values (it once marked a phase complete at 5/7 plans).

context_notes: This session's through-line: STALE BUT PLAUSIBLE RECORDS. Five separate planning artifacts were true when written and wrong when read — the checkpoint's '24 commits ahead of main' (the branch was already merged), the backlog todo's recommended fix (would have broken the gate it was meant to repair), CONTEXT D-A2 (the /print defect was fixed ONE DAY after CONTEXT was gathered), CLAUDE.md's generator-drift table (said four, now five), and the orchestrator's own partial-conversion count (claimed 6; a run-time parse of the fragments found 20 — following it would have shipped 12 unqualified PASS attestations over partially-covering tests). The only reliable defence was re-deriving from source at the moment of use. Every layer caught something the layer below missed, and the top layer was the orchestrator — which is the argument for instructing subordinate agents to distrust the brief they are handed. Also worth carrying forward: three plans' SUGGESTED red-proof mutations were inadequate because they turned something ELSE red; a mutation that fails the wrong assertion is worse than no mutation, because it looks like proof.
